h1:
Pattani Food Plan
Khao Yam, Nasi Dagang, Morning Tea & Kai Kolae in 3 Days
intro: Pattani is a city where sleeping in means missing the good stuff, because a lot of the local cooking is breakfast food that sells out before mid-morning. There's nasi dagang, khao yam with budu sauce, kopi tea shops where people are chatting before the sky even lightens, and kai kolae in coconut-cream sauce that tastes like the real deep-south borderlands. We mapped out a meal-by-meal plan across 3 days, picking places that Pattani locals actually go to, with opening hours and rough prices as far as we could check — so you can time it right and catch the good food before it's gone.

blocks.html: Pattani food is mostly Malay-Muslim cooking — bold, fragrant with spices, and almost all halal. What makes it fun to eat is that many dishes are tied to time of day: nasi dagang and tea are morning food, khao yam works for both breakfast and afternoon, and kai kolae shows up from late morning into the evening. Get the order of your meals right and you can knock out several local dishes in a single day without rushing.

blocks.title: Before you go
blocks.html: Pattani sits in Thailand's deep-south border provinces. Before you actually travel, it's worth checking the latest news and official safety/situation advisories from government sources. Plan to be out mainly during daylight, and keep in mind that many shops close on Fridays or religious holidays. Dressing modestly and respecting Muslim-Malay customs will make the trip more comfortable for everyone.

blocks.text: Pattani local eats you'll want to hit

blocks.html: Before the day-by-day plan, here's the shortlist of shops and dishes we'd want you to lock in first, ordered by how often locals mention them and whether you can actually find them right now. Prices are rough ranges — adjust for the dish and the time you go.

items.name: Nasi Dagang Sabarang
items.blurb: Nasi dagang is steamed rice eaten with a coconut-cream tuna curry and sambal — a classic breakfast across the three southern provinces. The Sabarang shop behind Benjama Rachuthit School has been at it for over 30 years: well-balanced flavor, easy on the wallet. The only catch is it sells out fast.
items.meta: Breakfast · around 06:00–09:00 (sometimes gone earlier) · closed Fridays

items.name: Kama Khao Yam Raja
items.blurb: Khao yam served with a basket of side vegetables, tossed with fragrant budu sauce and eaten with grilled fish rubbed in salt and turmeric. It's a legendary khao yam spot that Pattani locals rank near the top, over in the Anorou area on Na Kluea Road.
items.meta: Anorou area · opens afternoons, around 15:00–22:00 (closed some days)

items.name: Kai Kolae Yiyoh, Ramkomut
items.blurb: Grilled chicken doused in a southern-style coconut-cream curry sauce, spicy with a hint of sweet. This old-timer on Ramkomut Road is known for its traditional recipe with real first-press coconut cream and no MSG — it's the name people reach for when they talk about Pattani kai kolae.
items.meta: Ramkomut area · late morning to evening

items.name: Kai Kolae Kamoh, Ramkomut Soi 4
items.blurb: Another well-known spot in the Ramkomut area. Besides kai kolae, there's blood cockles that nearly every table orders on top — a good pick alongside Yiyoh if you want to compare two recipes.
items.meta: Ramkomut Soi 4 · late morning to evening

items.name: Kopi Bang Tea Shop (Cha Chak & Coffee)
items.blurb: A morning tea shop of the kind Pattani locals sit at to chat before the day starts. There's pulled-foam cha chak, dark kopi black coffee, eaten with roti and dumplings — the classic old-school kopitiam vibe you'll find all over town.

items.name: Tuen Ma Kor Cha Yen
items.blurb: A proper southern tea shop with bold, just-sweet-enough tea, plus breakfast dishes and sandwiches. A good stop to top up on caffeine morning or evening, on Kasemsuk Road in the Sabarang area.
items.meta: Kasemsuk Rd, Sabarang · morning 06:30–09:30, evening 17:00–19:00 · closed Sundays

items.name: Pantai Roti Cha Chak
items.blurb: A snacks-and-eats spot in the Rusamilae area with khao yam, roti, jae-mae, and cha chak. It's somewhere you can settle in for a while if you want to try several things in one place.

items.name: Murtabak (deep-south snack)
items.blurb: Square roti pastry wrapping spiced beef or chicken with onions and egg, fried until crisp outside and soft inside. You'll find it at tea shops and morning markets — a filling little snack worth trying.

items.name: Halal Dim Sum (Masreeya Dimsum)
items.blurb: Halal Muslim dim sum for anyone who wants dim sum with their morning kopi without worrying about the ingredients. It's another face of the Chinese-Malay culture in this city.

items.name: Morning & day markets in town
items.blurb: If you don't want to commit to one shop, walking the morning market gets you the full spread of local eats — fish congee, chicken biryani, Malay home-style sweets, and southern fruit. It's a cheap way to taste a lot of things.
items.meta: Several spots in town · early morning to mid-morning

blocks.html: Note: the opening hours and prices are based on the latest reviews we could find. Local shops change their hours often and many close on Fridays, so before you actually go, call ahead or check the shop's page again — better than showing up to a closed door.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Easy start, from nasi dagang to kai kolae

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Start with breakfast food, finish with kai kolae

items.activity: Start the day at Nasi Dagang Sabarang
items.note: It sells out fast, so go before 8. Order nasi dagang with tuna and egg, and have a hot tea with it.

items.activity: Move on to a nearby kopi tea shop
items.note: Sip dark kopi or cha chak, order roti or dumplings to fill up, and soak in the morning kopitiam atmosphere.
Old Chinese-Malay buildings, a mosque, and long-standing shops. Take photos and let your stomach rest up for the next meal.

items.activity: Khao Yam Raja (if it opens afternoons, push this to early afternoon)
items.note: Khao Yam Raja opens afternoons, so it may not be open at noon — pick another khao yam spot in town instead. Toss the vegetables thoroughly with the budu sauce.

items.activity: Kai kolae on Ramkomut (Yiyoh or Kamoh in Soi 4)
items.note: Open from late morning to evening. Order thigh, drumstick, and chicken skin, and try the cockles at Kamoh — get the coconut-cream sauce nice and saucy.

items.activity: Wind down along the Pattani River
items.note: A walk to settle the meal and catch the cool evening breeze. If you still have room, swing by an evening tea shop for one more round.

blocks.title: Pace your meals
blocks.html: On day one, don't stack heavy meals back to back. Nasi dagang and kai kolae are both bold and rich, so leave the old-town walk to empty your stomach before the afternoon meal — it'll taste better.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Tea, khao yam, and snacks

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: An easy day built around tea, roti, and khao yam

items.activity: A serious morning tea at Tuen Ma Kor Cha Yen, or your favorite kopi spot
items.note: Bold southern tea — order it with breakfast or a sandwich and sip your way into the morning.

items.activity: Walk the morning market in town
items.note: Try fish congee, chicken biryani, and Malay home-style sweets, and grab some snacks to take along.

items.activity: Pantai Roti Cha Chak, Rusamilae area
items.note: Order butterfly-pea khao yam or herb khao yam with roti and cha chak. You can settle in comfortably for a while.

items.activity: Take a break at a café in town
items.note: Hide from the afternoon sun, top up on dessert or coffee, before heading out for the evening meal.

items.activity: Try murtabak and halal dim sum as a snack
items.note: Beef or chicken murtabak, fried hot, with a hot tea — a light meal before dinner.
If you didn't get kai kolae on day one, today's your chance — or pick Muslim seafood in town.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Mop up what you haven't tried yet

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: A flexible day to catch missed shops + souvenirs

items.activity: Back to nasi dagang one more time (in case you missed round one)
items.note: If you went too late the first day and it was gone, set an alarm today to make up for it.

items.activity: A new tea shop you haven't tried
items.note: This city has plenty of tea shops — switch it up and compare kopi and cha chak across places.
Bottled budu sauce, Malay home-style sweets, and dried goods to take home — pick them up from the market or a souvenir shop in town.
Pick the spot you loved most from the past two days and go back for a repeat to scratch the itch.

blocks.html: If you only have a day or two, just cut day 3 — the core eats (nasi dagang, khao yam, morning tea, and kai kolae) are all covered in the day 1–2 plan. Day 3 is there for anyone who wants seconds or missed a shop that was closed the day before.

blocks.text: Tips for eating well in Pattani

items: Breakfast food sells out fast — nasi dagang and the popular tea shops start selling before the sky lightens, and some are running low by 7–8 a.m. Set an alarm to be safe.
Many shops close on Fridays — it's an important religious day, so a lot of Muslim shops are shut. Plan around it or check before you head out.
Carry cash — most local shops and market stalls take cash. Some have PromptPay, but not all of them.
Bold and spicy — southern Malay food packs heat. If you're not great with spice, tell the shop ahead of time, or order a sweet tea to cut it.
Mostly halal — most shops are halal, so alcoholic drinks are hard to come by. Plan accordingly.

blocks.text: Pairing food with sights between meals

items.name: Anorou old town
items.blurb: Old Chinese-Malay buildings, vintage shops, and a mosque — a perfect stroll while you wait for the afternoon spots to open.

items.name: Pattani Central Mosque
items.blurb: A key city landmark with handsome architecture, worth a photo stop during the day (dress modestly).

items.name: Pattani Riverside
items.blurb: A spot to walk off a heavy meal and catch the cool breeze — an easygoing atmosphere in the evening.

faq.q: What Pattani foods should I try?
faq.a: The mainstays are nasi dagang (rice with coconut-cream tuna curry, a breakfast dish), khao yam with budu sauce, the morning kopi and cha chak tea shops, and kai kolae in coconut-cream sauce in the Ramkomut area. Those four are the backbone of a Pattani food plan.

faq.q: Where's the best nasi dagang, and what time does it open?
faq.a: The one people mention most is Nasi Dagang Sabarang, behind Benjama Rachuthit School — it's been going for over 30 years. It opens early, around 6 a.m., and usually sells out before 9; some days it's gone by 7. It's typically closed on Fridays, so go early.

faq.q: Which Pattani kai kolae shops are famous?
faq.a: Ramkomut Road is the home of the old-school kai kolae spots — there's Yiyoh (traditional recipe with real first-press coconut cream) and Kamoh in Soi 4, which is also known for its cockles. Most open from late morning into the evening.

faq.q: Is it safe to visit Pattani right now?
faq.a: Pattani is in Thailand's deep-south border provinces. Before you actually travel, check the latest news and official safety/situation advisories from government sources, plan to be out mainly during daylight, and respect the local Muslim-Malay customs.

faq.q: Are there recommended morning tea shops in Pattani?
faq.a: There are several, like Kopi Bang (Cha Chak & Coffee) and Tuen Ma Kor Cha Yen in the Sabarang area, which serve bold southern tea with breakfast. The tea shops open early and are where Pattani locals sit and chat before the day begins.
